neighbours.label: Word-initial fragment (a lone letter like ' N', ' n', ' H', ' h', ' v', or '-h') that begins a rare, foreign or split-up word, strongest in food and menu text (dish names, recipe lines) and in the middle of a menu or list item.
fire: For lunch the café served a bright salad nicoise with tuna, olives and soft-boiled egg, plus a glass of rosé.
The tasting menu ended with a plate of hachis parmentier, rich with beef and a crust of browned potato.
Dinner last night was leftover rice and beans; I nuked some of it in the microwave while the kettle boiled.

Appetizers:
- Gougères (cheese puffs)
- Nems with fresh mint and lettuce
- Vichyssoise, served cold
Our grandmother always started the meal with a bowl of vichyssoise before the roast arrived.
The recipe calls for two cups of drained cannellini beans, a pinch of salt, and a spoonful of nduja stirred in at the end.
At the festival stall they sold hand-pulled noodles, nasi goreng, and little paper cones of hummus with warm bread.
The Jewish month of Nisan arrives in spring, and families begin preparing the house for the holiday weeks ahead.

The tasting menu ended with a plate of roasted beef, rich with gravy and a crust of browned potato.

The recipe calls for two cups of drained white beans, a pinch of salt, and a spoonful of tomato paste stirred in at the end.

short: split-word initial letter, esp. dish names
notes: 10x pilot (concept-maps/tenx, census arm): label and 16 sentences written by a fresh Sonnet 5.5 subagent from a packet (card + all-pole band samples + concept-census evidence (which concepts and domains selected the pole)); no probes. An Opus gate checked rule-level items only (8 + 8, 0 overlap with census and probe text, near misses free of the declared trigger) and edited nothing. Labeller's note: Strong activations are mostly a lone word-initial letter token starting a split rare/foreign word (nicoise, hachis, nuked, Nisan, 'u'zhin), with a food/menu skew that matches the census (61% of foods); a few top hits are ordinary words (' large', ' New'), so coverage is likely partial. Near misses use common whole-word equivalents in the same food frames.
